content.why_it_matters: Advanced Gaps-and-Islands Queries matters because database behavior becomes more reliable when the intended row meaning, data shape, and edge cases are explicit. This lesson follows the SQL curriculum's listed subtopics and calls out PostgreSQL-specific behavior when it matters.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: In advanced gaps-and-islands queries, define the unit of analysis before writing the query: one row per customer, order, day, or other grain. Make filters, NULL handling, time boundaries, and tie-breaking rules visible in the SQL.

content_blocks.title: Apply the idea

Define the result you expect, run or inspect the small example in your own disposable PostgreSQL lab, and change one assumption at a time. The embedded lesson editor is a demonstration shell: the current project shows the sample expected output and does not execute arbitrary SQL on the server.

items.title: Detecting consecutive dates
items.text: Detecting consecutive dates needs a clearly defined time zone and calendar grain. Prefer typed date/time values over formatted strings, define inclusive/exclusive boundaries, and check daylight-saving or month-boundary cases where they matter.

items.title: Grouping continuous intervals
items.text: Grouping continuous intervals helps you use SQL for reporting and analysis with the right grain, time buckets, windows, distribution statistics, and business metric definitions. Start with a concrete example, state the expected result, and verify the behavior before extending the query or design.

items.title: Finding gaps in sequences
items.text: Finding gaps in sequences changes how data is represented or exposed. Check dependencies, name objects consistently, keep structural changes in reviewed migrations, and rehearse the operation against a disposable copy before production.

items.title: Combining grouping logic and window functions
items.text: Combining grouping logic and window functions is easier to reason about when the input row grain, partition keys, ordering, and tie-breaking rule are explicit. A window expression can add a calculation while keeping the individual input rows visible.

content_blocks.code:
SELECT department_id, full_name, salary,
       DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY department_id ORDER BY salary DESC) AS salary_rank
FROM employees
ORDER BY department_id, salary_rank, employee_id;
content_blocks.expected_output: Employees remain individual rows and receive a salary rank within each department; equal salary values share a DENSE_RANK.

content_blocks.title: Remember
content_blocks.text: SQL correctness depends on data shape, constraints, NULL behavior, row counts, and the target database dialect—not just whether a statement parses.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a query is correct because it returns some rows.
common_mistakes.why: A result can omit valid records, multiply joined rows, mishandle NULLs, or rely on a non-deterministic order.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the expected row grain, add targeted edge cases, and use a stable tie-breaker whenever order or pagination matters.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying PostgreSQL syntax into another SQL engine without checking support.
common_mistakes.why: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, SQL Server, and Oracle differ in types, functions, row limits, procedural features, and transaction behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Label the target engine/version and verify the relevant official reference before adapting the query.

common_mistakes.problem: Testing with production data or credentials.
common_mistakes.why: Practice statements can change rows or expose sensitive information if run against the wrong connection.
common_mistakes.fix: Use a dedicated disposable lab, check current_database() and current_user, and review all changes before committing.
